channel.description: Recent content in World Heritage on Japan Specialty Traveler

item.title: Mozu Tombs: The Giant Keyhole Kofun of Sakai — Guide
item.description: The Mozu Tombs in Sakai are a group of giant burial mounds built in the fifth century for the rulers of early Japan, inscribed together with the nearby Furuichi group as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The greatest of them, the Daisen Kofun, is traditionally attributed to Emperor Nintoku: a keyhole-shaped mound 486 metres long, ringed by moats, its scale rivalling the Great Pyramid and the tomb of the First Emperor of China.

item.title: Tenryuji: Arashiyama's Great Zen Temple and Borrowed-Scenery Garden — Guide
item.description: Tenryuji is the most important temple in Arashiyama and one of Kyoto’s five great Zen temples, founded in 1339. While its wooden halls have burned and been rebuilt many times, its garden survives from the fourteenth century essentially unchanged — a masterpiece by the monk-designer Muso Soseki. Centred on a pond, it uses the technique of shakkei, ‘borrowed scenery’, drawing the wooded slopes of the Arashiyama hills into the composition so that garden and mountain read as one.

item.title: Toji: Kyoto's Tallest Pagoda and Great Flea Market — Guide
item.description: Toji, ‘the East Temple’, was founded in 796 when Kyoto became the capital and given to the great monk Kukai, who made it a centre of esoteric Shingon Buddhism. Its five-story pagoda, rebuilt in 1644, rises 55 metres and is the tallest wooden tower in Japan, a landmark visible from the shinkansen and an emblem of the city. Inside its Lecture Hall stands a three-dimensional mandala of twenty-one carved deities arranged by Kukai himself.

item.title: Himeji Castle: Japan's Finest Surviving Castle — Guide
item.description: Himeji Castle is the greatest surviving castle in Japan and one of the finest in the world: completed in its present form in 1609, it escaped the fires, sieges, demolition orders and wartime bombing that destroyed almost every other Japanese castle, and stands today entirely original. Its brilliant white plastered walls and layered gables earned it the nickname Shirasagi-jo, the White Heron Castle, and its defensive design — a spiralling maze of gates, walled lanes and dead ends climbing to the six-storey keep — is as impressive as its beauty.

item.title: Koyasan (Mount Koya): The Sacred Mountain of Shingon Buddhism — Guide
item.description: Koyasan, high in the forested mountains of northern Wakayama, is the spiritual heart of Shingon Buddhism and one of Japan’s most extraordinary places to visit. Founded in 816 by the monk Kukai — posthumously Kobo Daishi — as a remote monastic retreat, the mountaintop basin now holds a whole town of around 100 temples, a World Heritage Site where daily monastic life continues much as it has for twelve centuries. Visitors come to walk the vast cedar-shaded cemetery of Okunoin, see the great halls of the Danjo Garan and Kongobu-ji, and above all to stay overnight in a temple lodging, joining the monks for vegetarian cuisine and dawn prayers.

item.title: The Kumano Kodo: Japan's Ancient Pilgrimage Trails — Guide
item.description: The Kumano Kodo is a network of ancient pilgrimage routes threading the mountains of the Kii Peninsula, walked for over a thousand years by emperors, monks and commoners alike on their way to the three grand shrines of Kumano. Registered as a UNESCO World Heritage Site — one of only two pilgrimage routes in the world so listed, alongside Spain’s Camino de Santiago — its stone-paved paths climb through deep cedar forest, past moss-covered oji shrines and mountain hamlets.

item.title: Gangoji: The Ancient Temple Within Naramachi — Guide
item.description: Gangoji is one of Nara’s quietest World Heritage treasures, tucked into the lanes of Naramachi — the merchant quarter that in fact grew up within this once-vast temple’s former grounds. Gangoji traces its origins to Asuka-dera, Japan’s very first full-scale Buddhist temple founded in 588, and when the capital moved to Nara the temple moved with it. Though far smaller today, its main hall (Gokurakubo) is a National Treasure, and remarkably some of its roof still bears original tiles from the Asuka period, over 1,400 years old — among the oldest roofing in the world — making a modest visit a brush with the very dawn of Japanese Buddhism.

item.title: Heijo Palace: The Heart of Japan's Ancient Capital — Guide
item.description: Heijo Palace was the political and ceremonial heart of Heijo-kyo, Japan’s capital through most of the 8th-century Nara period, and its vast excavated site — a green plain on the northern edge of the city — is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Long left as archaeological fields, it has been brought vividly to life by full-scale reconstructions: the towering vermilion Suzakumon main gate, the majestic Daigokuden (Former Imperial Audience Hall) where the emperor once held state ceremonies, and a garden and excellent museums explaining daily life in the ancient capital.

item.title: Horyuji: The World's Oldest Wooden Buildings — Guide
item.description: Horyuji, in the quiet town of Ikaruga southwest of Nara, is one of the most important temples in Japan and among the most significant in the Buddhist world: founded by Prince Shotoku, the great early patron of Japanese Buddhism, in 607, its central Kondo (Golden Hall) and five-story pagoda are the oldest surviving wooden buildings anywhere on Earth, standing for over 1,300 years. Registered in 1993 as one of Japan’s first UNESCO World Heritage Sites, the temple preserves an unrivalled trove of early Buddhist art and architecture across its Western and Eastern precincts, a serene pilgrimage into the very origins of Japanese civilisation.

item.title: Kasuga Taisha: The Lantern Shrine in the Sacred Forest — Guide
item.description: Kasuga Taisha, founded in 768 as the tutelary shrine of the powerful Fujiwara clan, is one of Nara’s most atmospheric sites: a vivid vermilion shrine set deep within the Kasugayama primeval forest, reached along a wooded approach lined with some 2,000 moss-covered stone lanterns. Inside, around a thousand bronze lanterns hang from the eaves, and twice a year — at Setsubun in February and Obon in August — all 3,000 are lit at once for the Mantoro festival, filling the shrine with flickering gold.

item.title: Kasugayama Primeval Forest: Nara's Sacred Ancient Woodland — Guide
item.description: Rising behind Kasuga Taisha, the Kasugayama Primeval Forest is one of the most remarkable green spaces in Japan: a genuine virgin forest protected since 841, when hunting and logging were banned to honour the shrine’s gods, and left untouched for nearly 1,200 years. The result is a rare surviving lowland primeval woodland of towering evergreens, ancient cedars and dense undergrowth, alive with birds and deer, forming part of Nara’s World Heritage listing.

item.title: Kofukuji: The Five-Story Pagoda of Nara — Guide
item.description: Kofukuji, founded by the Fujiwara clan and moved to Nara in 710, was once among the most powerful temples in Japan, and its five-story pagoda — at 50 metres the second-tallest wooden pagoda in the country — is an icon of the city, rising beside Sarusawa Pond at the very entrance to Nara Park. Beyond the pagoda and the rebuilt Central Golden Hall, the temple’s greatest treasure is its National Treasure Museum, home to a celebrated collection of ancient Buddhist sculpture including the beloved three-faced, six-armed Ashura statue, one of Japan’s most admired religious artworks.

item.title: Mount Yoshino: Japan's Greatest Cherry-Blossom Mountain — Guide
item.description: Mount Yoshino (Yoshinoyama), in southern Nara, is celebrated as the greatest cherry-blossom destination in all of Japan: some 30,000 cherry trees, planted over more than a thousand years as sacred offerings, cover its slopes and bloom each spring in staggered waves that climb the mountain from the Shimo (lower) grove to the Oku (upper) grove over about two weeks. The effect — whole ridgelines washed in shifting pink, dotted with temples and shrines — is breathtaking, and the mountain is also a sacred centre of Shugendo mountain asceticism and part of a UNESCO World Heritage listing.

item.title: Todaiji and the Great Buddha: Nara's Colossal Temple — Guide
item.description: Todaiji is the grandest of Nara’s temples and one of Japan’s most awe-inspiring sights: founded in 752 as the head of all provincial Buddhist temples, it houses the Daibutsu, a 15-metre seated bronze Great Buddha, one of the largest bronze statues in the world, enshrined within the Daibutsuden — for centuries the largest wooden building on earth. The approach passes through the towering Nandaimon gate, guarded by a pair of ferocious 8-metre Nio guardian statues carved in the 13th century, while sacred deer roam the grounds.

item.title: Toshodaiji: The Temple of the Blind Master Ganjin — Guide
item.description: Toshodaiji, in Nishinokyo near Yakushiji, was founded in 759 by Ganjin (Jianzhen), the revered Chinese monk who, after five failed attempts and the loss of his eyesight, finally reached Japan to establish proper Buddhist ordination — a story of extraordinary devotion. His temple is one of Nara’s most serene: its Kondo (Golden Hall), built in the classical Tenpyo style with a colonnade of eight great pillars, is considered one of the most beautiful ancient buildings in Japan, and the temple grounds, quieter and more wooded than most, hold a lacquered seated statue of Ganjin himself, a National Treasure shown to the public just a few days each year.

item.title: Yakushiji: The Twin-Pagoda Temple of Nishinokyo — Guide
item.description: Yakushiji, in the Nishinokyo district west of central Nara, was founded in the late 7th century by an emperor praying for his consort’s recovery, and remains one of Japan’s most beautiful temple complexes. Its signature is symmetry: a pair of elegant three-story pagodas (that appear to have six roofs each) flank the Kondo hall, the East Pagoda an original 8th-century survivor and the West Pagoda a vivid modern reconstruction. Within the Kondo sits the Yakushi Triad, a magnificent bronze Medicine Buddha flanked by two bodhisattvas, counted among the supreme masterpieces of early Japanese Buddhist art.

item.title: Kumano Kodo Iseji: The Pilgrimage Route Through Mie — Guide
item.description: The Kumano Kodo is a network of ancient pilgrimage routes across the Kii Peninsula, registered as a UNESCO World Heritage site, and its Iseji route is the one that runs through Mie — linking the great shrine of Ise with the sacred Kumano region down the prefecture’s rugged southern coast. Walked by pilgrims for over a thousand years, the Iseji climbs a series of atmospheric mountain passes paved with moss-covered cobblestones, threading through towering cedar forest between glimpses of the Pacific.

item.title: Onigajo: The Demon's Castle Sea Cliffs of Kumano — Guide
item.description: Onigajo, the ‘Demon’s Castle’, is a spectacular stretch of coastline near Kumano in southern Mie, where centuries of wind, waves and tectonic uplift have carved the cliffs into a surreal landscape of honeycombed hollows, jutting terraces and cave-like recesses stacked in tiers above the crashing Pacific. A walking path threads along and through the formations, and the site — part of the Kumano Kodo pilgrimage World Heritage area — comes wrapped in legend as the lair of a demon slain by a hero of old.

item.title: Miho no Matsubara: The Legendary Pine Grove With Mount Fuji Views — Guide
item.description: Miho no Matsubara is a seven-kilometre stretch of coastline planted with some 30,000 pine trees, framing one of Japan’s most celebrated views: Mount Fuji rising across the waters of Suruga Bay beyond the black-sand beach and twisted pines. The grove is a component site of Mount Fuji’s UNESCO World Heritage listing and the setting of the famous Hagoromo legend, in which a celestial maiden left her feathered robe hanging on a pine here, a story still honoured at the ‘Hagoromo pine’ and in Noh theatre.

item.title: Shiraito Falls: A Curtain of Fuji Spring Water — Guide
item.description: Shiraito Falls, near Fujinomiya at the southwestern foot of Mount Fuji, is one of Japan’s most graceful waterfalls, its name meaning ‘white threads’ after the hundreds of silky streams of water that pour over a curved, 20-metre-high and 150-metre-wide cliff face. Almost all of the water is Mount Fuji’s rain and snowmelt, filtered through the volcanic rock for decades before emerging from the cliff itself, and the falls are a component site of Fuji’s World Heritage listing, long revered as a place of worship and purification.

item.title: Mount Fuji UNESCO World Heritage Sites: The Sacred Mountain's Cultural Legacy — Guide
item.description: Mount Fuji was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2013 not as a natural wonder but as a cultural site, recognised as a ‘sacred place and source of artistic inspiration’ that has shaped Japanese religion, art and identity for centuries. The designation includes numerous component sites across the mountain’s northern foot in Yamanashi, from the Fujisan Hongu Sengen shrines that served as bases for pilgrim ascents, to the Fuji Five Lakes, Oshino Hakkai springs and other sacred natural features tied to Fuji worship, offering visitors a way to understand the mountain’s deep cultural significance beyond the view alone.
